title: Electrocatalytic Reduction of Gaseous CO2 to CO on Sn/Cu‐Nanofiber‐Based Gas Diffusion Electrodes
abstract: DOI: 10.1002/aenm.201901514 CO partial current densities of 144[6g] and 147 mA cm−2,[7a] respectively. Here, we investigate the electrocatalytic performance and stability of a GDE design for the electrocatalytic reduction of gaseous CO2 employing earth-abundant tin/copper (Sn/Cu) catalysts. Sn-decorated Cu surfaces were shown previously to provide high selectivity for CO2 to CO conversion in aqueous electrolyte and achieve CO partial current densities of up to 11.5 mA cm−2.[8] However, at higher current densities, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) starts to dominate due to insufficient CO2 supply.[8b] To enhance CO2 mass transport, we develop a process to fabricate electrospun polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) nanofibers with uniform Cu coating, and employ electrochemical underpotential deposition (UPD) of Sn to decorate the Cu surface. We demonstrate that Sn/Cu-coated PVDF (Sn/Cu-PVDF) nanofiber GDEs have CO faradaic efficiencies (FEs) above 80%, and achieve high CO partial current densities of up to 104 mA cm−2, representing the highest reported current density for a Sn/Cu-based catalyst for CO2RR to CO. We employ electrospun PVDF nanofiber membranes as templates for fabricating freestanding Cu-nanofiber electrodes (Figure 1; Figure S1, Supporting Information). The PVDF surface is activated by grafting a self-assembled polydopamine (pDA) layer.[9] The pDA layer provides nuclei for electroless Cu deposition from a precursor consisting of 50 × 10−3 m Cu(II) ethylenediaminetetraacetate (Cu-EDTA) and 0.1 m borane dimethylamine complex. After a reaction at 35 °C for 2 h, conformally Cu-coated PVDF (Cu-PVDF) nanofibers form a conductive network with a sheet resistivity lower than 2.41 Ω. UPD, providing 2D deposition control, is employed to decorate the Cu-PVDF nanofibers with Sn. Control over the exact amount of Sn is critical to obtain high selectivity for CO2RR to CO.[8a,b] On CO-selective Sn/Cu catalysts, the initial intermediate of the CO2RR is proposed to bind to the surface via the carbon (*COOH).[8g,10] When the amount of Sn on the Cu surface exceeds the optimal value, CO2 binds to the surface preferentially via the oxygen forming a bidentate *OCHO intermediate,[8g,10] and behaves similarly to a Sn electrode which is selective for HCOO−.[8c–g,11] To quantify the coverage of deposited Sn by UPD, we make use of a polycrystalline Cu rotating disk electrode with an electrochemical surface area of 0.686 cm2. Sn UPD from an Ar-saturated 1 × 10−3 m SnSO4 + 0.1 m H2SO4 solution correlates to the reduction peak tailing to Earth-abundant Sn/Cu catalysts are highly selective for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CO in aqueous electrolytes. However, CO2 mass transport limitations, resulting from the low solubility of CO2 in water, so far limit the CO partial current density for Sn/Cu catalysts to about 10 mA cm−2. Here, a freestanding gas diffusion electrode design based on Sn-decorated Cu-coated electrospun polyvinylidene fluoride nanofibers is demonstrated. The use of gaseous CO2 as a feedstock alleviates mass transport limitations, resulting in high CO partial current densities above 100 mA cm−2, while maintaining high CO faradaic efficiencies above 80%. These results represent an important step toward an economically viable pathway to CO2 reduction.

sections.heading: Sn/Cu-Nanofiber Electrodes
sections.text:
The electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) powered by renewable electricity represents a promising pathway to produce renewable carbon-based feedstock and synthetic fuels.[1] In particular, several techno-economic analyses proposed the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to carbon monoxide (CO) or formate/formic acid (HCOO−/HCOOH) to be economically most viable.[2] Cost competitive CO2 electrolysis for CO requires a high CO partial current density (>150 mA cm−2) at low overpotentials (<1 V), and stable long-term operation (>8000 h).[3] Due to the low solubility of CO2 in water (≈34 × 10−3 m at 1 bar and 25 °C[4]), the current density for CO2RR is limited to ≈20 mA cm−2 using dissolved CO2 as reactant.[5] The use of gaseous CO2 as the feedstock for CO2RR alleviates CO2 mass transport limitations, enabling much higher current densities. Gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) employing silver (Ag)[5,6] and gold (Au)[7] as catalysts in neutral pH media were shown to achieve
Adv. Energy Mater. 2019, 1901514

−0.2 V (vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)) in cyclic voltammograms (CVs) (Figure S2e, Supporting Information). From the transferred charge in the reduction peak, an electrochemical surface area of Sn is estimated to be 0.131 cm2, resulting in a Sn coverage of ≈0.2 mono layer, which agrees with Yan et al.[12] Sn/Cu-PVDF electrodes are prepared by Sn UPD at −0.2 V for 200 s (Figure S3, Supporting Information).
Figure 1a,b shows scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of a PVDF membrane before and after metal deposition, respectively. The diameters of PVDF nanofibers before coating follow a Gaussian distribution with a mean value of 270 nm, while the mean value of diameters increases to 364 nm after Cu and Sn deposition (Figure S4a, Supporting Information). Assuming uniform growth of the Cu layer along the radial direction, we estimate the average thickness of the Sn/Cu layer as ≈47 nm, consistent with the cross-sections of the Sn/Cu-PVDF nanofibers prepared by a focused ion beam (FIB) milling and subsequently imaged by SEM revealing the core–shell structure in Figure 1c. A sketch of the composition of all layers in a nanofiber deduced from the fabrication process is shown in Figure 1e. In the high-resolution SEM shown in Figure 1d, a bright ring placed between a dark core and a surrounding gray ring can be observed. We identify the bright ring with the originally deposited metal layer with a thickness of about 50 nm, and the surrounding gray ring with a milling artifact redeposited during FIB milling.
The CO2 pressure drop through the 8 µm thick Sn/Cu-PVDF electrode is measured at different CO2 face velocities from 10 to 100 cm min−1 (Figure 1f). Applying Darcy's law, we extract an intrinsic permeability of 1.8 × 10−14 m2 for CO2.[13] The geometric parameters of the Sn/Cu-PVDF electrode, including the thickness and the distribution of nanofiber diameters, are acquired by analyzing their top-view and cross-sectional SEM images (Figure S4c,d, Supporting Information). Based on the intrinsic permeability and the geometric parameters, we generate a virtual 3D fibrous model for the Sn/Cu-PVDF electrode with dimensions of 15 µm × 15 µm × 8 µm (inset in Figure 1f). The details for modeling and simulations are provided in the Supporting Information. This model indicates that the porosity of the Sn/Cu-PVDF electrode is 77%, and the typical pore sizes range from 0.5 to 0.9 µm (see red diamonds in Figure S12 in the Supporting Information). The simulated CO2 pressure drop across the fibrous model fits very well to the experimental results. Figure 1g visualizes the 3D pressure field for an 85.7 Pa pressure drop through the electrode at a face velocity of 80 cm min−1.
Elemental mapping of the Sn/Cu-PVDF electrode by energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) (Figure 2a; Figure S5a, Supporting Information) shows that Cu, carbon (C), fluorine (F), oxygen (O), and nitrogen (N) are located along the nanofibers. F stems from the PVDF, and Cu from the metal layer. Interestingly, the N signal, originating from 5,6-dihydroxyindole in

pDA,[9b] also matches the nanofiber topography, confirming the existence of a pDA interlayer between PVDF and Cu. Elemental mapping of cross-sections of Sn/Cu-PVDF nanofibers encapsulated in an epoxy resin (Figure 2b; Figure S6, Supporting Information) confirms that all PVDF nanofibers, both in the outermost layers and in the bulk of the membrane, are conformally coated by Cu. Figure 2c shows the EDS spectrum of Sn/Cu-PVDF nanofibers encapsulated in an epoxy resin. A trace amount of Sn can be identified, but its intensity is too low for mapping.
Figure 2d compares the CVs of Cu-PVDF and Sn/Cu-PVDF electrodes recorded in Ar- or CO2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 solutions. The CVs of Cu-PVDF show oxidation peaks with onsets at 0.07 and 0.38 V, corresponding to the adsorption of OH− on Cu and the formation of Cu2O, respectively.[14] In contrast with the CVs of Cu-PVDF, an additional pair of peaks can be observed in the CVs of Sn/Cu-PVDF in the potential range from −0.35 to 0.51 V, which are assigned to the redox pair SnO/SnO2.[8b,15] For CVs recorded in CO2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3, oxidation of SnO to SnO2 requires higher polarization, and the magnitude of the pair of peaks decreases, indicating that a competing chemical
process takes place in the presence of CO2 that prevents the redox reactions of Sn oxides.[15]
The design and principle of operation of the membrane– electrode assembly (MEA) for half-cell testing is presented schematically in Figure 3a. Details of the fabrication process are provided in the Supporting Information. A Sn/Cu-PVDF nanofiber electrode, acting as a freestanding GDE, is pressed onto an anion exchange membrane (AEM). Gaseous CO2 diffuses through the GDE to the electrode/membrane interface, and is thereby reduced. Gaseous products (e.g., CO) flow out of the GDE. Liquid products and anions (e.g., HCO3− and OH−) diffuse through the AEM to the anolyte (0.1 m KHCO3). Both the reference and the counter electrodes are immersed in the anolyte. Figure 3b shows a cross-sectional SEM image of a Sn/Cu-PVDF/AEM assembly prepared by hot pressing at 125 °C. The AEM used in this work has a three-layer structure with a carrier of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) sandwiched between two polystyrene tetramethyl methylimidazolium (PSTMIM) membranes.[16] Figure 3c compares the CVs of a Sn/Cu-PVDF GDE exposed to Ar or CO2 atmosphere. The potentials for the redox pair SnO/SnO2 are similar with those

obtained in Ar- or CO2-saturated 0.1 KHCO3 solutions. At the applied potentials ≤−0.32 V, the current density increases significantly, corresponding to the onset of the HER in Ar atmosphere and particularly to the onset of the electrochemical conversion of CO2RR to CO in CO2 atmosphere.
The performance of Sn/Cu-PVDF GDEs is assessed by supplying a continuous CO2 gas flow in the cathodic compartment and quantifying gaseous products by gas chromatography. Figure 4a summarizes the FEs for the gaseous products, including hydrogen (H2), CO, and ethylene (C2H4), as a function of the applied potential. Individual chronoamperograms for all potentials normalized to the geometric surface area and the FEs for each individual sampling point are provided in Figure S7 in the Supporting Information. The sum of the FEs for gaseous products falls only slightly below 100%, indicating that no significant amount of liquid products is formed. The partial current densities and the production rates for the gaseous products are shown in Figure 4b,c, respectively. The HER is efficiently suppressed on the Sn/Cu-PVDF, corresponding to current densities below 9.0 mA cm−2, and production rates lower than 0.16 mmol h−1 cm−2. In contrast, the FEs for CO are above 80% at potentials ≤−0.9 V, and the partial current densities for CO increase continuously up to 104 mA cm−2 at −1.2 V, resulting in a CO production rate of 1.94 mmol h−1 cm−2. At potentials ≤−1.0 V, detectable amounts of C2H4 emerge with FEs less than 8.2%, corresponding to current densities lower than 10 mA cm−2 and very low production rates of ≤0.03 mmol h−1 cm−2. The formation of C2 species (C2H4 and CH3CH2OH) on a Sn/Cu surface at high overpotentials was already observed in our previous study,[8b] indicating that the Sn/Cu surface retains some of the original features of pure Cu.[17]
The long-term stability of the Sn/Cu-PVDF GDE was investigated by chronoamperometry at −1.0 V for 135 h. Gaseous products were analyzed every 59 min. Figure 4d shows the chronoamperogram. Electrolysis starts at an initial geometric current density of ≈60 mA cm−2, and maintains values of 60 to 70 mA cm−2 during the first 70 h. To avoid an accumulation of liquid products in the anolyte, the anolyte was replaced several times during the 135 h by fresh CO2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3
at the moments marked by red dashed lines in Figure 4d. The used anolyte was kept for proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) analysis. Even after extended operation of 135 h, the current density remains above 40 mA cm−2. The loss of current density coincides with the increase of the ohmic resistance in the MEA (Figure S8, Supporting Information), while the loss of active sites on the GDE cannot be excluded. The Sn/Cu-PVDF GDE maintains high selectivity for CO2RR over the 135 h (Figure 4e). The average FE for CO is 84.9%, while the average FEs for H2 and C2H4 are 10.6% and 4.4%, respectively. The 1H NMR spectrum from the used anolyte employed during the last interval (Figure S9, Supporting Information) shows that the anolyte contains a small, but quantifiable amount of HCOOH, and trace amounts of acetate (CH3COOH), ethanol (CH3CH2OH), propionaldehyde (CH3CH2CHO), and 1-propanol (CH3CH2CH2OH). These liquid products are generated at the electrode/membrane interface, and they diffuse through the AEM, and accumulate in the anolyte. The average FE for HCOOH is 2.1%, while the proportion of other liquid products is significantly less than 1% FEs in total.
To investigate the influence of CO2 mass transport on the current density during the CO2RR, we prepared a Sn/Cunanofiber GDE with a lower intrinsic permeability. Figure S10 in the Supporting Information shows the SEM images of a Sn/ Cu-polycaprolactam (Cu/Sn-nylon) electrode prepared using a dense electrospun nylon nanofiber membrane as a template. In contrast to the 8 µm thick Sn/Cu-PVDF electrode, which exhibits an intrinsic permeability of 1.8 × 10−14 m2, the 2.5 µm thick Sn/Cu-nylon electrode (see Figure S11 in the Supporting Information), consisting of finer and more compact nanofibers, has a significantly lower intrinsic permeability of 3.5 × 10−15 m2. The performance of Sn/Cu-nylon GDEs for CO2RR has also been evaluated with the MEA design prepared as described above (see Figure S13 in the Supporting Information). With a less efficient CO2 mass transport, the Sn/Cu-nylon GDE reaches lower CO partial current densities, with the highest recorded value of only 63.7 mA cm−2 at −1.2 V (Figure S14b, Supporting Information). The ratio of CO2 fluxes of 160% through the Sn/Cu-PVDF versus Sn/Cu-nylon GDE is

in excellent agreement with the ratio of the CO2 consumption rates of 155% determined by the production rates of the two major carbon-based gaseous products (CO and C2H4) at −1.2 V, indicating that the production rate is limited by CO2 diffusion to the reaction zone at the electrode/membrane interface (see Section 9 in the Supporting Information). Interestingly, the H2 partial current density of the Sn/Cu-nylon GDE increases significantly from an average value of 3.4 mA cm−2 (−0.7 to −1.0 V) to 11.0 mA cm−2 at −1.2 V, indicating the ineffectiveness of the electrode in suppressing the HER. Although the HER does not dominate at −1.2 V, its FE rises above 10%, while the FE for CO drops below 80% (see Figures S14a and S15h in the Supporting Information). This result is consistent with the observation in our previous study under reducing conditions, where the Sn/Cu surface requires efficient CO2 supply to maintain high CO selectivity.[8b] The CO partial current densities measured at our Sn/CuPVDF and Sn/Cu-nylon electrodes are compared with results from literature (neutral electrolyte only) in Figure 5. The performance of our GDEs based on an earth-abundant catalyst is comparable to those of Ag-based GDEs. In conclusion, we have produced Sn/Cu-nanofiber electrodes as freestanding GDEs for the electrocatalytic reduction of gaseous CO2 to CO. We exploited the underpotential deposition of Sn on Cu to precisely control the Sn coverage, resulting in high CO selectivity. For Sn/Cu-PVDF electrodes, the obtained FEs for CO at potentials ≤−0.9 V are above 80%, and for the first time Sn/Cu-electrodes achieve a CO partial current density >100 mA cm−2. CO selectivity is maintained above 80% at −1.0 V even after extended operation of 135 h. We have further demonstrated that a high intrinsic permeability of the Sn/Cu nanofiber GDEs is critical for maintaining high CO2 to

While our results represent an important step toward an economically viable CO2 reduction, further studies are needed to reach the threshold of >150 mA cm−2 at overpotentials <1 V for >8000 h identified by techno-economic analyses.
